idiom_name: hand-written frame loop over a receive buffer (getline/getdelim + one send per part)
implementation_notes: C has no iterator protocol, messaging runtime or reflection, so nothing replaces the classic structure: the splitter is an explicit loop that consumes one framed composite (getdelim() for delimiter-terminated records, or a length prefix decoded with memchr()/memcpy() off a recv() buffer), serialises each part into its own buffer and hands it to the transport. Correlation id, sequence number and sequence size must be written into the part header by hand, because no framework fills them in - that metadata is what a later aggregator or resequencer consumes. The loop form is not a simplification of the pattern but its smallest complete realization; a Splitter struct with a table of function pointers only pays off when several payload formats must share one pipeline, which is exactly the configuration the classic component form exists for.
pitfalls: getline()/getdelim() reuse and resize the caller's buffer: every part must be copied (or reference-counted) before the next read, otherwise all parts alias the same memory.
A frame split across two read()/recv() calls needs a stateful accumulation buffer; treating each read as one message silently truncates parts at packet boundaries.
There is no back-pressure at this level - a tight split loop outruns the socket or exhausts memory unless the send blocks or is bounded.
Sequence counters and per-composite state must live in the call, not in file-scope statics; a shared counter produces duplicate correlation metadata for concurrent splits.
